notes.front: What is test automation?
notes.back: The conversion of test activities to automated operation.
notes.explanation: The definition speaks of test activities in general, not only of running tests.
notes.example: Like a factory replacing a worker who inspects bottles by eye with a camera that checks each one.
notes.evidence: The conversion of test activities to automated operation.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test automation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: Which type of test tool makes the test process more efficient by helping to manage the lifecycle, requirements, tests, defects and configuration?
notes.back: Test management tools.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says they increase the efficiency of the test process.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool supports testers in performing reviews and static analysis?
notes.back: Static testing tools.
notes.explanation: They support examining work products without running them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool helps to generate test cases, test data and test procedures?
notes.back: Test design and test implementation tools.
notes.explanation: They support producing the testware needed before execution.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool supports automated test execution and measuring coverage?
notes.back: Test execution and test coverage tools.
notes.explanation: The syllabus groups running tests and measuring their coverage together.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool lets testers perform non-functional testing that is hard or impossible to do by hand?
notes.back: Non-functional testing tools.
notes.explanation: Some non-functional testing cannot practically be done manually.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool supports the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking and automated builds?
notes.back: DevOps tools.
notes.explanation: They support continuous integration and delivery too.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which type of test tool exists to make communication easier?
notes.back: Collaboration tools.
notes.explanation: The syllabus describes them simply as tools that facilitate communication.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Virtual machines and containerisation tools belong to which type of test tool?
notes.back: Tools supporting scalability and deployment standardisation.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives these two as its examples.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can an ordinary spreadsheet count as a test tool?
notes.back: Yes, when it is used to assist in testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus counts any tool that assists in testing as a test tool.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The syllabus’s list of test tool types is {{c1::not complete}}: it gives examples only.
notes.explanation: It introduces the list with “examples include, but are not limited to”.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which test tool topics did syllabus v4.0 remove as too advanced for Foundation Level?
notes.back: Tool selection, pilot projects and introducing tools into an organisation.
notes.explanation: The v4.0 release notes list this among the major changes to chapter 6.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, “Release notes for the 4.0 version”, p. 75
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does simply acquiring a test tool guarantee success?
notes.back: No: a new tool pays off properly, and keeps paying off, only if effort is put into it.
notes.explanation: Buying the tool is only the start.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, what are two kinds of effort a new test tool needs?
notes.back: Any two of: tool introduction, maintenance and training.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives these as examples of the effort needed for lasting benefits.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the syllabus say must happen to the risks a test tool brings?
notes.back: They need analysis and mitigation.
notes.explanation: Tools bring risks as well as benefits.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of test automation comes from cutting repetitive manual work, such as re-running regression tests?
notes.back: Time saved.
notes.explanation: Re-entering the same data or comparing results by hand are other repetitive jobs a tool can take over.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of test automation comes from greater consistency and repeatability?
notes.back: Prevention of simple human errors.
notes.explanation: A tool does the same steps in the same order each time.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of test automation concerns objective assessment, such as coverage, and measures too complicated for people to work out?
notes.back: More objective assessment.
notes.explanation: The tool measures rather than a person judging.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of test automation gives statistics, graphs and aggregated data on test progress and failure rates?
notes.back: Easier access to information about testing.
notes.explanation: This information supports test management and test reporting.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do reduced test execution times from automation lead to?
notes.back: Earlier defect detection, faster feedback and faster time to market.
notes.explanation: Tests that finish sooner report sooner.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does test automation free testers’ time for?
notes.back: Designing new, deeper and more effective tests.
notes.explanation: Time no longer spent on repetitive work can go to test design.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation concerns what people believe a tool will deliver, including its features and ease of use?
notes.back: Unrealistic expectations about the tool’s benefits.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names functionality and ease of use as things people may expect too much of.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation concerns the time, cost and effort to introduce a tool, maintain test scripts and change the manual process?
notes.back: Inaccurate estimates of them.
notes.explanation: All three kinds of effort can be underestimated.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation arises when manual testing would have been more appropriate?
notes.back: Using a test tool anyway.
notes.explanation: Not every test is better done by a tool.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation involves ignoring the need for human critical thinking?
notes.back: Relying on the tool too much.
notes.explanation: A tool does not replace testers’ judgement.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation arises if the supplier goes out of business, retires or sells the tool, or gives poor support?
notes.back: Dependency on the tool vendor.
notes.explanation: Poor support can mean weak answers to queries, upgrades or defect fixes.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation concerns open-source software?
notes.back: The project may be abandoned, leaving no updates, or its parts may need updating quite often as it develops.
notes.explanation: Abandoned software gets no further updates.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation concerns the tool and the development platform?
notes.back: The tool may not be compatible with the development platform.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists platform incompatibility among the potential risks of test automation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which risk of test automation concerns regulatory requirements and safety standards?
notes.back: Choosing an unsuitable tool that does not comply with them.
notes.explanation: Compliance is part of whether a tool is suitable.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tool simulates 10,000 shoppers using a web shop at once to measure response times. Which type of test tool is it?
notes.back: A non-functional testing tool.
notes.explanation: Load on this scale is difficult or impossible to produce manually.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tool flags unused variables and risky constructs in source code without running it. Which type of test tool is it?
notes.back: A static testing tool.
notes.explanation: It performs static analysis.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tool records which lines of code were exercised while the automated suite ran. Which type of test tool is it?
notes.back: A test execution and test coverage tool.
notes.explanation: Measuring coverage belongs to this type.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.1 “Tool Support for Testing”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company buys an expensive automation tool and expects savings from the first month, with no training or script upkeep planned. What does the syllabus say about this?
notes.back: A: acquiring a tool does not guarantee success; it needs effort, such as training and maintenance.
notes.explanation: Real and lasting benefits need effort for introduction, maintenance and training.
notes.choices:
A) Acquiring a tool does not guarantee success; it needs effort, such as training and maintenance
B) The plan is sound, because automation always saves time
C) Tools only need effort when they are open-source
notes.choicesExplained: B hardens a potential benefit into a certainty. C has no basis: every new tool needs effort.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After automating its regression suite, a team learns the morning after a change whether it broke anything, instead of a week later. Which benefit of test automation is this?
notes.back: Reduced test execution times, giving earlier defect detection and faster feedback.
notes.explanation: Faster runs report their results sooner.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 59
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team’s automated suite has passed for months, so nobody reviews what it checks any more, and a serious defect slips through untested. Which risk of test automation is this?
notes.back: C: relying on the tool too much.
notes.explanation: Ignoring the need for human critical thinking is the syllabus’s example of over-reliance.
notes.choices:
A) Dependency on the tool vendor
B) The tool is not compatible with the development platform
C) Relying on the tool too much
notes.choicesExplained: A concerns the supplier, who is not involved here. B would stop the tool working, but it runs fine.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A medical-device team picks a test tool that does not meet the safety standard its product must follow. Which risk of test automation is this?
notes.back: A: choosing an unsuitable tool that does not comply with regulatory requirements or safety standards.
notes.explanation: Failing a required safety standard makes the tool unsuitable.
notes.choices:
A) Choosing an unsuitable tool that does not comply with regulatory requirements or safety standards
B) Unrealistic expectations about the tool’s benefits
C) Using open-source software that may be abandoned
notes.choicesExplained: B is about expecting too much, not about compliance. C concerns abandoned open-source software, which the scenario does not mention.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 6.2 “Benefits and Risks of Test Automation”, p. 60
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
